transcript: As Cats the JELLICLE ball can closes on Broadway, I wanna bring up a point of view that I've mentioned a few times before when this sort of passion project closes on Broadway. And of course, I know it's ironic to call this revival of a hugely successful musical a passion project. But you know that it is, and you know why it is. So I'm not gonna sit here and say that you shouldn't be sad that it's closing. I'm sad that it's closing. I was the number one complainer that it didn't win best revival. Obviously, you want it to run a long time, for people to see it, to be financially successful, to employ all of these artists, many of whom don't usually get a voice on Broadway. So, yes, absolutely. It's a shame. And I think a lot of the time when people point out that Broadway is such a cutthroat industry that, like, you know, some really high percentage of shows fail commercially, they mean that in a way of, like, suck it up, get over it. But there's a big silver lining to me, which is that, like, Broadway producers and investors know that. They know that most shows fail commercially. They know they're probably not gonna get their money back. And they knew that cats the musical was gonna be a tough sell for a long, sustainable run. They knew all of that when they decided to take it to Broadway anyway. And Yeah, there's broader contextual issues with that. Like, I wish this weren't an industry where a lot of these productions feel like they need the stamp of Broadway to get the platform and visibility that they want. I wish that the financial model wasn't built in such a way that producers and investors feel like they have to choose between a passion project and a cash cow. But it is still encouraging that amidst the cash cows, there are still producers and investors choosing the passion project.
classificationReason: Reaction to the show's closing on Broadway and discussion of Broadway economics; no first-hand review of the production itself.
